newsitem.title: USA: Clinton discusses foreign policy with lawmakers.
newsitem.headline: Clinton discusses foreign policy with lawmakers.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton lobbied members of the Senate on Wednesday to support approving a chemical weapons treaty as the administration sought backing in Congress for its foreign policy.
Clinton and his top foreign policy advisers were to meet with several dozen members of Congress on Wednesday night for talks that were to range from NATO enlargement to engagement with China.
White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Clinton made telephone calls to about 10 members of the Senate to enlist their support in winning approval of a treaty outlawing chemical weapons.
The accord takes effect on April 29, and the administration argues that the United States will be at a serious disadvantage if the pact has not been ratified by then.
Approval was considered "very much up in the air at this point," said White House National Security Adviser Sandy Berger. "There is some strenuous opposition from some groups."
Sen. Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has been a leading critic of the chemical weapons accord. He declined to attend the Wednesday night dinner meeting.
Officials said Clinton wanted to meet with lawmakers at the Blair House, an official government guest residence across Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House, in an informal setting over dinner.
"It's a very important opportunity for both the president and the congressional leadership to build a kind of bipartisan consensus around America's leadership in the world," Berger said.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Defence Secretary William Cohen and National Security adviser Samuel Berger were scheduled to participate.

The session comes at a time when the administration is struggling to get the Middle East peace process back on track, despite a new cycle of violence between Israel and the Palestinians, and to expand the NATO alliance without alienating Russia.

It is also embroiled in controversy over the 1996 Clinton re-election campaign's fund-raising tactics -- a controversy that has raised questions about possible illegal efforts by China to funnel money into the campaign in order to buy U.S. political influence.
Chinese officials have denied any interference in the U.S. political process.
